title: What Lily Was and Was Not
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
The first time I asked Snape whether he had been in love with Lily or in love with what she represented, he nearly choked on tea.

We were at Spinner's End, sitting on the floor because the terrible chair had finally collapsed under a repair charm and Snape was taking this as a personal insult.

He set down his cup.

“What an appalling question.”

“Too personal?”

“Too imprecise.”

I smiled.

“That sounds promising.”

“It should not.”

I had not planned to ask.

The question had been circling since the hearing, sharpened by newspapers that kept reducing Lily to a symbol in Snape's story and Snape to a symbol in hers.

I did not want to do the same.

“You can refuse,” I said.

“I am aware.”

He leaned back against the wall.

The sitting room smelled of dust and fresh plaster. One of his laboratory plans lay open on the floor between us.

“At eleven,” he said, “I loved her because she was kind to me.”

I stayed quiet.

“At fifteen, I loved her because she was clever and stubborn and because she had become part of how I imagined my own future.”

His face tightened.

“At sixteen, I loved her badly.”

The words were simple.

“What does that mean?”

“I wanted her understanding without giving sufficient respect to what she objected to. I resented people she cared for because I believed my history with her should matter more than her choices.”

James.

Her friends.

The people Snape had hated or dismissed.

“And later?”

“Later I loved someone who was dead.”

His eyes moved toward the window.

“That makes honesty difficult.”

“Because she couldn't change?”

“Yes.”

The answer surprised me with its clarity.

“Memory preserves what it preserves. Grief edits. Regret edits more.”

I thought of the girl in the Pensieve. Laughing. Angry. Defending her sister. Refusing his apology when it was not enough.

“She wasn't a saint,” I said.

Snape's eyes flashed.

“No.”

The force of agreement made me smile.

“What?”

“You sounded offended on her behalf.”

“I am offended by most simplifications.”

“Consistent.”

He looked down at his tea.

“Lily could be impatient. Judgmental. Reckless when angry. She enjoyed being right more than she admitted.”

“You liked that.”

“Sometimes.”

“You hated it when it was aimed at you.”

“Yes.”

“Also consistent.”

His mouth twitched.

I shifted closer, our shoulders touching against the wall.

“Do you think she would forgive you?”

Snape became very still.

The reporter had asked that.

I regretted the question immediately.

“Sorry.”

“No.”

I looked at him.

He was not refusing.

He was answering.

“No?”

“I do not know,” he said. “And I no longer believe I am entitled to construct an answer for her.”

That felt important.

“For years I imagined what she would say because there was no one to contradict me.”

His expression tightened.

“That is not conversation. It is ventriloquism.”

I let the words sit.

“So you stopped?”

“I am trying to.”

I took his hand.

He looked at our fingers.

“Does being with me feel disloyal to her?” I asked.

His head snapped toward me.

“No.”

Immediate.

My chest loosened.

“Did it ever?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I appreciated the truth more than a prettier answer.

“When?”

“The first time I wanted to kiss you.”

“In Hogsmeade?”

“Earlier.”

I blinked.

“How much earlier?”

He looked annoyed.

“Why is that relevant?”

“Severus.”

The name slipped out naturally.

We both froze.

I had called him Snape almost from the beginning. He had called me whatever the moment allowed: Consultant, occasionally a ridiculous nickname based on some professional error, more often nothing at all because names were unnecessary in a room built for two.

His first name felt intimate in a way kissing had not.

“Again,” he said quietly.

My pulse jumped.

“Severus.”

His eyes closed for half a second.

When they opened, he looked younger and older at once.

“The first time,” he said, “was the night you caught the memory vial.”

I stared.

“That early?”

“I did not say I wanted to act on it.”

“You wanted to kiss me.”

“I considered the possibility.”

“That is Snape for wanted to kiss me.”

“Do not become unbearable.”

“Too late.”

I was grinning.

He looked deeply irritated and slightly embarrassed.

It was wonderful.

Then his expression sobered.

“I felt disloyal because desire seemed like movement.”

“Away from her?”

“Yes.”

“And now?”

“I understand movement is not replacement.”

I squeezed his hand.

“Good.”

His gaze sharpened.

“You were worried.”

“Of course I was.”

“You said neither of us was required to compete with the dead.”

“I meant it. That doesn't mean I'm incapable of insecurity.”

He studied me.

“What were you afraid of?”

That question was harder to answer.

I looked at the cracked plaster on the opposite wall.

“That I would become evidence that you were healed.”

Snape's expression changed.

“Explain.”

“That people would look at us and say, see, he moved on, so everything is fine now. Or that you'd look at us that way.”

His face hardened with something like offense.

“I would never use you that way.”

“I know that now.”

“And before?”

“I didn't know anything before.”

A fair point.

He looked down.

“You are not proof of recovery,” he said.

The sentence warmed me unexpectedly.

“You are not a cure. You are not a reward. You are not a substitute.”

Each word precise.

“What am I?”

His mouth tightened.

“A person asking irritating questions on my sitting-room floor.”

I laughed.

Then he added, “Whom I love.”

Everything stopped.

No build-up.

No speech.

He looked as startled as I felt.

“Severus.”

“Do not.”

“You just—”

“I am aware.”

“You said—”

“I am aware.”

His face had gone red.

I was smiling so hard it hurt.

“This is unbearable,” he muttered.

“I love you too.”

Silence.

His eyes snapped to mine.

The room changed.

Not because love was new.

Because language had caught up.

Snape looked down at our hands.

“Are you certain?”

“No.”

His face fell.

I squeezed his fingers.

“I mean I can't prove it in a laboratory. I can't tell you the exact day it started. I can't promise what we'll be in ten years.”

I leaned closer.

“But yes. I love you.”

His expression cracked into a small, helpless smile.

“Pedantic,” he said.

“You taught me.”

“I regret everything.”

“Liar.”

He kissed me.

Slowly.

The laboratory plans crumpled under my knee.

Neither of us cared.

Later, we smoothed them out on the table.

Lily remained part of his life.

So did I.

Those facts did not need to destroy each other.

Both could be true.
